aspects.says: Fork/Join is the tool for CPU-bound decomposition, and virtual threads are the tool for I/O-bound concurrency.
Forking both subtasks and joining both costs an extra fork per split and leaves the current thread only waiting in join.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: The canonical pattern forks one subtask, computes the other in the current thread, then joins.
aspects.reason: practised on its own pages: sum-task on 6.6.1.2 builds the pattern and join-last on 6.6.1.4 checks that the join comes last; not drafted twice

aspects.says: RecursiveTask and RecursiveAction extend ForkJoinTask, which implements Future.
aspects.reason: background taxonomy; using a ForkJoinTask as a Future is practised by run-all and within on page 6.6.1.1

aspects.says: invokeAll() forks and joins several tasks at once and is preferred for RecursiveAction.
aspects.reason: practised by scale and tree-totals on page 6.6.1.3; percent here uses it for its in-place step

aspects.says: Java 19 added setParallelism(), lazySubmit() and close(), so a ForkJoinPool works in try-with-resources.
aspects.reason: API additions listed for reference; shutting a custom pool down is practised by isolated on page 6.6.1.1 and stream-in-pool here

aspects.says: Calling join() on a task that was never forked or invoked blocks forever, because nothing will run it.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: the only thing a test can observe is a hang, which it can only time out on; every practice of the module forks or invokes each task it joins

aspects.says: Blocking on I/O or locks inside a fork/join task defeats work-stealing, so it goes through ManagedBlocker or another pool.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: practised by managed-block on page 6.6.1.1, which blocks through ForkJoinPool.managedBlock

aspects.says: A fork/join computation can first produce a result, such as the largest value, and then change the array in place using it.
Subtasks avoid data races by combining results at join time or by using atomic accumulators.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: practised by min-max on page 6.6.1.2 (results combined at join) and count-matching on page 6.6.1.3 (an atomic accumulator)

aspects.says: Parallel streams run in the JVM-wide common pool unless the stream operation is submitted as a task to a custom pool.
RecursiveTask<V> is used when the computation's result is needed and RecursiveAction for an in-place transformation.
aspects.reason: which task type a solution picks cannot be seen by any test, since a RecursiveTask can also change an array in place; the percent practice follows the page's pairing, and the choice is taught by page 6.6.1.3's action practices

aspects.says: A threshold decides when to stop splitting, and a good one balances task overhead against parallelism.
aspects.reason: practised by adaptive-threshold and split-tree on page 6.6.1.4, whose subject is the threshold

aspects.says: Null, empty and single-element arrays are handled as base cases, and a negative parallelism is refused.
aspects.reason: minor guards; ForkJoinPool's own constructor already refuses a parallelism below 1, and the empty array is a case of the percent practice

aspects.says: Each worker has its own deque, and idle workers steal tasks from the tail of busy workers' deques.
aspects.reason: which worker steals which task is up to the scheduler, so no test can observe it deterministically; it is asked in the quiz of page 6.6.1.4
